Newborn Care

Feeding support for babies with a cleft or low muscle tone

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Some babies need extra help to feed safely and take enough milk. The right support starts with the baby’s anatomy and abilities, while keeping your own feeding wishes and wellbeing in the conversation.

Start with a plan for your own baby

A cleft lip, cleft palate or low muscle tone can change how a baby attaches, draws milk and coordinates sucking, swallowing and breathing. Down syndrome may involve low tone and other health needs, but feeding ability varies. Twins or other multiples can also bring practical challenges without having the same feeding mechanics.

Ask an infant-feeding clinician or the cleft team to observe a feed. The plan should cover safe swallowing, enough milk, your comfort and how progress will be reviewed. Looking attached or spending a long time at the breast is not proof of adequate intake.

Breast milk and closeness can take different forms

Breast milk provides nutrition and immune components and is associated with a lower risk of some infections. These benefits can matter to babies with additional health needs, but they do not guarantee protection from viruses, asthma or allergies. Other medical care remains important.

Direct breastfeeding can be convenient when it works well, but convenience should not be assumed for every family. A baby who cannot transfer enough milk may receive expressed breast milk, formula or other prescribed nutritional support. Needing that help does not cancel the value of the milk you can provide.

Sucking uses the muscles of the mouth and jaw, but it is not a proven promise of better later speech. Speech development has many influences and may need its own specialist support. Skin-to-skin time, close holding and responsive feeding can support your relationship whichever feeding route is safest.

Cleft lip is different from cleft palate

With a cleft lip alone, the main challenge may be forming a seal around the breast. Many babies can breastfeed with positioning support. Breast tissue may help fill the lip opening, and a specialist can show whether gentle support near the lip helps your baby.

A cleft in the palate affects the separation between the mouth and nose, making the suction needed for milk transfer more difficult. The size and position of the cleft matter, but even a convincing-looking latch can deliver little milk. A small opening should not be assumed to be closed by a hand position.

Many babies with a cleft palate need a specialist bottle or another feeding method. Direct breastfeeding, comfort at the breast or expressed milk can still be discussed as part of the individual plan. The priority is enough nutrition without exhausting the baby.

What the Dancer hand hold supports

The Dancer hand hold is a way of supporting the breast and the baby’s chin and jaw together. It may help some babies with low muscle tone. It is not a treatment that repairs or reliably seals a cleft palate.

In the general hand arrangement, the middle, ring and little fingers support the breast from below. The space between the thumb and index finger provides support for the chin, while those two fingers can gently support the sides of the jaw. The baby’s neck, shoulders and body also need support.

Have a feeding specialist demonstrate this with your baby and watch you practise. The exact angle and pressure depend on the baby’s anatomy and feeding assessment; do not squeeze the cheeks, press the throat or force the head into the breast. Keep the face visible and breathing unobstructed.

A supported, more upright position may be helpful in some circumstances, but there is no required same-arm or elbow placement that makes feeding safe for every baby. The hold is useful only if the baby remains comfortable and transfers milk effectively.

Feeding with Down syndrome or low muscle tone

Reduced jaw strength, tongue control or stamina can make it harder to maintain attachment and an effective suck. Some babies with Down syndrome breastfeed successfully; others need extra support, assessment or a different route for part or all of their milk.

Coughing, choking, slow feeds, poor growth or recurrent breathing symptoms need attention. Milk entering the airway can sometimes happen without obvious coughing, so the absence of a dramatic choking episode does not prove that swallowing is safe.

A skilled feeding assessment may lead to further swallow testing when indicated. Breathing or heart problems can also affect feeding endurance. A Dancer hold alone cannot resolve every coordination problem.

Choose positioning, pauses and timing together

Supported cradle, cross-cradle or under-arm positions are possible options. The best position needs to work for both of you and support safe, effective feeding; comfort alone cannot tell you how much milk is transferred. Ask for adjustments if your back, shoulders or healing incision hurt.

Some babies benefit from shorter efforts with pauses and more frequent opportunities, while others need more time. Do not impose a universal short-feed rule or end a feed before the agreed intake without a plan for the remaining milk. Ask how to recognise tiredness and when to stop or change approach.

Babies who swallow more air may benefit from pauses for burping. Gentle burping can be tried when the baby seems uncomfortable, but producing a burp after every feed is not a condition that must be met. Persistent distress or breathing difficulty needs assessment rather than more vigorous burping.

Protect milk supply and make extra feeding manageable

If milk transfer is limited, ask about hand expression or pumping to support supply. Agree on a workable schedule and how the expressed milk will be offered. A clinician should show you specialist bottles and explain pacing and flow; do not enlarge a teat or squeeze milk into the mouth without instruction.

Follow the prescribed supplementation plan and review it as feeding changes. Do not reduce extra milk simply because the baby stays longer at the breast. If additional calories or a change in milk consistency is needed, get an exact clinical plan rather than adding powder or thickener yourself.

Another caregiver may help with preparing equipment, recording feeds or offering milk by the agreed method. The plan needs to account for parental rest and access to equipment, not just a technically possible feeding routine.

Track growth and know when to get help

The care team may follow weight, wet nappies, alertness and feeding stamina closely. Ask what to record and when the next weight or feeding review will happen. Fewer wet nappies than expected, worsening tiredness or consistently poor intake needs prompt contact.

Stop the feed and seek emergency help if the baby struggles to breathe, becomes blue or grey, is unresponsive or cannot be woken normally. Repeated coughing or choking with feeds, poor growth or new respiratory symptoms needs prompt clinical review even if the baby settles between episodes.

After cleft surgery or another change in treatment, confirm the current feeding instructions with the team. Do not assume that the earlier equipment or positioning plan remains the best option.

Support includes your feelings about feeding

It is understandable to feel disappointed when feeding looks different from what you hoped. You can ask for support with that feeling as well as practical help. Needing expressed milk, specialist equipment, formula or tube feeding does not mean you have failed.

Ask the team to explain what is achievable now, which changes they expect with growth or treatment and how decisions will be reviewed. A flexible plan can preserve closeness while meeting the baby’s current needs.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Distinguish cleft lip from cleft palate and assess actual milk transfer.

Low tone and swallowing difficulties need individual assessment.

How BeMama can help

Ask for a demonstrated feeding plan, a follow-up date and clear signs that should prompt an earlier call. Practise with the team rather than relying on a diagram alone.

When to seek help

Stop a feed and seek emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unresponsiveness or abnormal difficulty waking. Repeated choking or poor intake needs prompt assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Breast milk can be offered through different routes.
  • A Dancer hold supports the jaw; it does not close a palate defect.
  • An apparent latch does not prove adequate intake.
  • Feed length and burping are individual decisions.
  • Safe growth and parental support matter more than one feeding technique.

Frequently asked questions

Can a baby with a cleft lip breastfeed?

Often yes, particularly with a cleft lip alone. A feeding assessment helps establish a seal and verify intake.

Can the Dancer hold seal a cleft palate?

No reliable seal or adequate intake can be assumed. Many babies need a specialist feeding method.

What does the Dancer hand position do?

It supports the breast and the baby’s chin and jaw. Learn the placement with a feeding specialist.

Does Down syndrome rule out breastfeeding?

No. Abilities differ, and some babies need support for low tone, stamina or swallowing.

Is swallowing safe if the baby never coughs?

Not necessarily. Some aspiration is silent, so poor growth or breathing symptoms also matter.

Should every feed be short?

No. Agree on timing, pauses and extra milk according to stamina and effective transfer.

Must the baby burp after every feed?

No. Offer gentle pauses as needed; do not force a burp or ignore persistent distress.

Will breastfeeding guarantee better speech?

No. Sucking uses oral muscles, but later speech depends on many factors and may need specialist support.

Can we stay close if direct breastfeeding is not possible?

Yes. Responsive feeding, holding and appropriate skin-to-skin time support closeness across feeding methods.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
